title: Bad Trips Guide, Round 2
intro: Your round-1 answers are in: the guide after round 1 is the file sent with this page, and every card's fate is recorded. This page carries out your structure answer, A: the Quick Bad Trip Checklist keeps each step's heading and one or two of your lines, step 1 keeps its danger signs in full, and each step ends with a link to the section that has the rest. The Longer Triage goes; the few things only it says move into the long part.

Three cards at the end turn your round-1 answers into lines (Q-3 and Q-6, in your words as far as I could keep them, and your advice to try the remedies in low doses first). Nothing changes until you approve it. Humanizing starts after this round, with your three new rules: AI quips go or get humanized, "one ordinary" goes everywhere, and "X does not Y" gets changed.

reads.text: 1. Is this medically or physically dangerous?

Trouble breathing, a prolonged or repeated seizure, collapse, inability to wake normally, dangerous overheating, severe or worsening chest pain, one-sided weakness, inability to speak normally, loss of bodily control, serious injury, repeated vomiting, a dangerous drug combination, or someone who cannot be kept physically safe?

Get urgent help while giving basic first aid and any appropriate immediate rescue measures. Medical help and field rescue can happen in parallel. Please don’t spiritually process a body that is going under.

reads.text: If someone says “my brain feels damaged”

Take that seriously even if they are high. Use DMSO immediately while checking whether they can stay awake, breathe normally, smile evenly, raise both arms, repeat a simple sentence, walk, control their bodily functions, and report seizure, severe headache, repeated vomiting, dangerous heat, chest pain, or vision changes. These checks include several recognized stroke warning signs.

If this is a psychedelic and the concern is actual brain damage rather than a trip that is merely too intense, I am no longer trying to preserve the trip: DMSO comes first, then Ipomoea pes-caprae to stop the trip cold and fast. For MDMA, move from DMSO to the magnesium-and-electrolyte branch.

edits.before: One hand on heart and one on belly.
Longer-exhale breathing.

Gentle Buteyko-style reduced breathing: breathe softly and slowly through the nose, taking in slightly less air than you want until there is only faint air hunger. No strain, no long breath-holds while intoxicated, and stop if it spikes fear.
Silence or one calm track on repeat.
Low light, a blanket, and simple reassurance.
Slow pacing or gentle movement when that reduces pressure.

Some people over-breathe during panic. The resulting low CO<sub>2</sub> can produce tingling, lightheadedness, and feelings of unreality that make the trip seem even more threatening. Gentle breathing reduction is meant to soften that loop, rather than become a new breathing project. Source: Johns Hopkins on hyperventilation.

edits.before: Activated charcoal has legitimate toxicology uses after some recent oral ingestions, but it isn’t a universal “I took too much” remedy. It matters what was swallowed, how recently, whether charcoal binds it, and whether the person is fully alert and can protect the airway. It can be dangerous when someone is vomiting, sedated, seizing, or unable to swallow safely. Source: clinical review on activated charcoal.

reads.text: 10. Is the gut the main problem?

Nausea, diarrhea, a dirty or toxic feeling, or a parasite-die-off feeling may need body-level support. But don’t let “toxins” distract from repeated vomiting, severe abdominal pain, dehydration, blood, fever, confusion, fainting, respiratory depression, collapse, seizure, dangerous overheating, or another concrete sign of poisoning.
My personal first thought here is ozonated zeolite rather than charcoal because charcoal can reduce the trip and bind many substances.

edits.before: The Longer Triage: What Kind of Trouble Is This?

When somebody is in trouble, the first question is simple: what could hurt them now? A body in danger, a person moving toward harm, and a frightened mind in a terrible room are different problems. Treating all three as “a difficult process” is how people end up trying to breathe through poisoning or calling an annoying song ancestral trauma.
image 2
Is the body failing—or is neurological status still unknown?

Breathing trouble, collapse, a seizure lasting five minutes or repeating without normal recovery, dangerous overheating, severe or worsening chest pain, one-sided weakness, loss of speech or bodily control, serious injury, signs of real poisoning, or a credible risk of harm to self or others means medical help while acting. This is the branch where time matters and presence alone is not the intervention. Don’t make somebody “sit with it” while a body is going under.

A person saying “my brain feels damaged,” “my brain is broken,” or “I’m losing control of my body” also belongs in this first branch until the symptoms are actively checked. The phrase is not a diagnosis. It is also not permission to call the problem anxiety because the person is high. Someone experiencing real neurological dysfunction may be unable to explain it more clearly.

Use DMSO immediately while asking what the symptoms actually are. Can the person stay awake, breathe normally, smile evenly, raise both arms, repeat a simple sentence, walk, and control their bodily functions? Is there seizure activity, one-sided weakness, speech loss, severe headache, repeated vomiting, dangerous heat, chest pain, or a vision change? If the person cannot answer reliably, basic stability remains unknown rather than reassuring.

If objective danger signs appear, use DMSO while somebody arranges medical help. If the screen is reassuring but the brain-damage feeling remains, continue the DMSO-first route and reassess promptly. With a psychedelic, safety now means stopping the trip with Ipomoea pes-caprae rather than merely calming it. With MDMA, move to magnesium and the broader electrolyte branch; I do not yet know whether pes-caprae works for MDMA.
Is the room making everything worse?
Too much light. Bad music. A hostile person. A sitter trying too hard—or doing nothing. Five people talking. A phone buzzing. The wrong temperature. No bathroom, privacy, or sense of safety.

A huge amount of what gets called “deep psychedelic crisis” is a nervous system begging for a less irritating room. Dim the light, lower the sound, stop the chatter, clear out extra people, offer water without forcing it, adjust the temperature, open bathroom access, stop touching unless touch is wanted, speak slowly, and please don’t explain the universe at someone who is scared. None of this is glamorous. It’s mercy.
Is this real emotional material?
Is the body writing the horror story?
Can love be reached yet?

This may be the deepest question, but it usually isn’t the first move. Someone who is too overwhelmed, frightened, sick, hot, or scrambled may be unable to reach “send love.” Stabilize first. Then love.

suggestions.title: What counts as stable, and the ER's limits, move under the rescue section's first paragraph
suggestions.what: The Longer Triage's stable-state test ("When the person is breathing normally, not dangerously hot, not seizing, has no neurological-injury concern, remains conscious enough to cooperate, and can be kept physically safe, calming and stabilizing the trip may be enough.") and its ER paragraph move under "An emergency means act now..." at the start of Acute Medical and Neurological Rescue. The ER paragraph loses "Calling for help is not the same thing as receiving good care." and "That is why the decision belongs to the actual symptom pattern rather than the word “overdose.”"

The test says what physically stable means, and the ER paragraph says why, so all three readers took them as one point. The first cut line changes nothing a reader does (reader C); the second is the ingestion section's ("“Overdose” is too vague to choose a remedy.").

edits.before: The emergency room is not magic, and for a physiologically stable psychedelic crisis it may be a poor environment. A scared, psychotic-feeling person often receives a benzodiazepine; those drugs don’t reliably address psychosis and can cause paradoxical agitation or fear in some people. Antipsychotics may work better for psychosis, but they carry their own risks and interactions, often administered by someone who doesn’t know what was taken. Calling for help is not the same thing as receiving good care. That is why the decision belongs to the actual symptom pattern rather than the word “overdose.”

suggestions.title: A possible bleed, in your words (your answer to Q-3)
suggestions.what: The stroke paragraph gains, after "...because the symptoms improved enough to feel reassuring.": "If someone is worried about a bleed, I'd probably skip DMSO, but it depends on how severe their issue is. It's not a powerful blood thinner like heparin, unless maybe injected; it's basically a dietary blood thinner. I've never had any issues with bleeding too much from consuming DMSO, and never heard of it either, but if bleeding is already a medical issue I'd want to think about that more."
suggestions.why: Your answer: "if someone is worried about a bleed, i'd prob skip dmso but it depends on how severe their issue is, it's not a powerful blood thinner like heperin or something unless maybe injected, it's a dietary blood thinner basically ... i've never had any issues with bleeding too much because of consuming dmso myself. never heard of it either but if that's already a medical issue i'd wanna think about that more". You asked me to check how strong it is: the human platelet study your chest-pain section already links found a mild effect in donated blood (platelets stuck about 15% less under flow, and aggregation fell about 6%), which fits "not a powerful blood thinner" (PubMed: [Asmis et al. 2010](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbrc.2009.12.102)). I found no study of bleeding in people taking it by mouth, so the line stays your experience.
suggestions.stays: The rest of the stroke paragraph.
suggestions.deciding: Whether it belongs here or with the DMSO section's blood-thinning line.

edits.before: For objective stroke-like signs, I would use DMSO immediately while someone calls medics. DMSO cannot identify whether the problem is a clot, a hemorrhage, low oxygen, an electrolyte crisis, or something else. The larger adjacent risk is losing a treatment window or missing a bleed because the symptoms improved enough to feel reassuring.
edits.after: For objective stroke-like signs, I would use DMSO immediately while someone calls medics. DMSO cannot identify whether the problem is a clot, a hemorrhage, low oxygen, an electrolyte crisis, or something else. The larger adjacent risk is losing a treatment window or missing a bleed because the symptoms improved enough to feel reassuring. If someone is worried about a bleed, I'd probably skip DMSO, but it depends on how severe their issue is. It's not a powerful blood thinner like heparin, unless maybe injected; it's basically a dietary blood thinner. I've never had any issues with bleeding too much from consuming DMSO, and never heard of it either, but if bleeding is already a medical issue I'd want to think about that more.
